findings.finalFix: ans: "Rapid expansion diluted the concept, quality varies widely within crus, and for decades leading houses (Trimbach, Hugel) refused to use it, labelling their best wines by brand instead (Clos Ste Hune, Jubilee). Both came round only recently (Trimbach Grand Cru Geisberg from the 2009 vintage, Hugel from 2015 with Grossi Laüe Grand Cru Sporen), which left the market unconvinced." findings.claim: The house holds that its names (Clos Sainte-Hune, Frédéric Émile) guarantee more than the cru system's politics — so the labels omit 'grand cru'
findings.finalFix: The house long held that its own names (Clos Sainte-Hune in Rosacker, Frédéric Émile from Geisberg and Osterberg) guarantee more than the cru system, so those flagships still omit 'grand cru'. Since the 2009 Geisberg (released 2015) it has also bottled Grand Cru Geisberg, Schlossberg, Mandelberg and Brand under the cru name.

findings.claim: Which grand cru's name means 'sorcerers' hill', beloved of Gewurztraminer at Zind-Humbrecht?
findings.finalFix: q: "Which Wintzenheim grand cru, whose name means 'stallion', is a Zind-Humbrecht Gewurztraminer site?"; ans: "Hengst"; accept: ["hengst"]; exp: "Hengst ('stallion' in German) is the grand cru of Wintzenheim, long reputed for Gewurztraminer on calcareous marl. Zind-Humbrecht also makes Gewurztraminer from Goldert ('golden') in Gueberschwihr. No Alsace grand cru has a name meaning sorcerers' or witches' hill."
